section_summary: This section documents efforts by American motion picture producers and distributors to address escalating Japanese import restrictions, exchange controls, and regulatory burdens following the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese conflict. It contains detailed representations and petitions from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan to Japanese officials and U.S. Ambassador Joseph C. Grew concerning unfulfilled film import agreements and millions of yen in frozen earnings, culminating in an appeal by the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America to Secretary of State Cordell Hull for official diplomatic intervention. The section also includes the text of relevant Japanese foreign exchange ordinances and the complete 1939 Enforcement Regulations of the Motion Picture Law, which imposed state licensing, political and cultural censorship, and strict foreign film exhibition quotas.

subfiles.about: Frederick L. Herron appeals to Secretary of State Cordell Hull to instruct the American Ambassador in Japan to file an official protest against Japanese film restrictions and the new Motion Picture Law.
subfiles.from: Frederick L. Herron, Foreign Manager, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.
keywords: Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America
subfiles.summary: Frederick L. Herron, Foreign Manager of the Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding restrictions imposed on American motion picture distributors in Japan. In light of the announced enforcement of a new Japanese motion picture law on January 1, 1940, and unfulfilled commitments by Japanese officials, he requests that the State Department file an official protest through Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. Herron encloses background documentation from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan detailing their negotiations and difficulties since Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Secretary of State Cordell Hull Requesting Diplomatic Protest

subfiles.about: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan submits a detailed memorandum to Ambassador Grew outlining problems concerning film import permits, the new Motion Picture Law, and frozen funds.
subfiles.from: R. D. Spierman, Honorary Secretary, American Motion Picture Association of Japan
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: Following an interview on November 13, 1939, the American Motion Picture Association of Japan submits a comprehensive report to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding their operational difficulties in Japan. The association explains that while remittances of 3,000,000 yen were permitted under an August 1938 agreement with the Finance Ministry, import permits for the remaining $10,000 of the agreed $30,000 print cost have been withheld, even though Japanese film exports to the U.S. continue unrestricted. They express deep concern over impending distribution quotas under the new Motion Picture Law and urge diplomatic representations to help release approximately 4,000,000 yen in accumulated frozen funds.
subfiles.title: Letter from American Motion Picture Association of Japan to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan

subfiles.about: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan appeals to former Finance Minister O. Kaya to use his good offices to secure the fulfillment of the August 1938 film import agreement.
subfiles.from: Chairman, American Motion Picture Association of Japan
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan writes to former Finance Minister O. Kaya expressing gratitude for his previous mediation while urging his assistance with the Exchange Control Bureau. Although fund remittances were completed under the August 10, 1938 agreement, the Finance Ministry had only granted permits for $15,000 worth of film imports out of the agreed $30,000. Warning that head offices in New York and Hollywood producers may interpret these continuing delays as bad faith, the association requests Kaya's influence to expedite the remaining permits and preserve friendly bilateral relations.
subfiles.title: Letter from American Motion Picture Association of Japan to O. Kaya
subfiles.to: O. Kaya, former Minister of Finance

subfiles.about: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan petitions S. Ikeda regarding delayed import permits, lack of replacement permits for censored films, and quota inequities.
subfiles.from: Chairman, American Motion Picture Association of Japan
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: One year after concluding their agreement with the Finance Ministry, the American Motion Picture Association of Japan petitions S. Ikeda regarding the unfulfilled balance of $12,500 in film import permits. The association emphasizes that Japanese films enjoy unrestricted entry and payment in the United States, in stark contrast to the severe restrictions placed on American films in Japan. They also request that replacement permits be allowed for films rejected by censors and that import allocations among individual member companies be distributed more equitably.
subfiles.title: Letter from American Motion Picture Association of Japan to S. Ikeda
subfiles.to: S. Ikeda, former Minister of Finance

subfiles.about: Kojiro Nakamura communicates the official conditions of the Department of Finance governing American film imports under credit and royalty remittances.
subfiles.from: Kojiro Nakamura, Head of Exchange Bureau, Department of Finance
subfiles.summary: Kojiro Nakamura, Head of the Exchange Bureau of the Japanese Department of Finance, notifies Michael M. Bergher of the official approval terms for importing American films under credit and remitting royalties. The terms permit film print imports up to $30,000 at a minimum cost of 1.5 cents per foot before the end of 1938, subject to monthly approval and exchange control ordinances. Royalties up to 3,000,000 yen may be remitted via the Yokohama Specie Bank to be held without interest in its San Francisco branch for three years before disbursement to parent companies.
subfiles.title: Official Notice from Kojiro Nakamura to Michael M. Bergher on Film Import and Remittance Agreement
subfiles.to: Michael M. Bergher, Representative of American Motion Picture Association of Japan

subfiles.about: A memorandum outlining the American Motion Picture Association of Japan's proposed terms for film importations, royalty remittances, and related operational needs.
subfiles.from: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: This memorandum produced by the eight member companies of the American Motion Picture Association of Japan sets forth their operational plan submitted to the Department of Finance. It details terms for remitting 3,000,000 yen in accumulated royalties over three years through the Yokohama Specie Bank and importing up to $30,000 in film prints before the end of 1938. The document also requests single joint permits for member companies, specific print cost rules for color films, permission to re-ship unimported prints, and sufficient supplies of raw film for making duplicates in Japan.
subfiles.title: Outline of Memorandum Produced by American Motion Picture Association of Japan

subfiles.about: Excerpts of Japanese Finance Department ordinances specifying legal restrictions and licensing requirements for foreign exchange transactions and import settlements.
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains English translations of excerpts from Japanese foreign exchange control legislation governing import settlements. It includes Article 1 of Finance Department Ordinance No. 1 of 1937, which restricts payments for foreign goods and establishes monthly exemption thresholds, and Article 4-(2) of the same ordinance, prohibiting importations without foreign exchange drafts except under specified exceptions. It also sets forth Article 3 of Finance Department Order No. 7 of 1933, barring unauthorized purchases of foreign currency, sales of foreign exchange, and overseas remittances.
subfiles.title: Excerpts of Japanese Department of Finance Ordinances on Foreign Exchange Control

subfiles.about: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan protests the suspension of film import permits resulting from objections by small Japanese distributors.
subfiles.from: Chairman, American Motion Picture Association of Japan
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan appeals to Finance Minister S. Ikeda following notification that film import permits under the August 10, 1938 agreement have been suspended due to pressure from independent Japanese distributing companies. The association objects to being equated with newly established local distributors who import inferior foreign films, arguing that major American studios represent leading cultural and entertainment forces. Emphasizing that two members have traveled to New York to help curb anti-Japanese sentiment in newsreels, the Chairman urges Ikeda to honor the agreement to avoid damaging bilateral friendship.
subfiles.title: Letter from American Motion Picture Association of Japan to Finance Minister S. Ikeda

subfiles.about: Official regulations detailing administrative procedures, licensing, censorship, and quotas for enforcing the Japanese Motion Picture Law.
subfiles.from: Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Education
subfiles.summary: This document provides an unofficial English translation of the administrative regulations promulgated by the Home and Education Ministries for enforcing Japan's Motion Picture Law. Articles 1 through 15 establish licensing, notification, and equipment standards for film producers and distributors, mandatory registration of directors, actors, and technicians, and child labor restrictions. Articles 16 through 34 set forth prize criteria, censorship standards for domestic and export films, and fee schedules, while Articles 35 through 58 establish compulsory educational film screenings, theatre operating rules, and an annual quota limit of 50 foreign dramatic prints per theatre.
subfiles.title: Regulations Concerning the Enforcement of the Motion Picture Law

subfiles.summary: This document is a duplicate copy of the American Motion Picture Association of Japan's November 16, 1939 letter to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. It details the history of the August 1938 agreement with the Finance Ministry, the impending enforcement of the new Motion Picture Law on January 1, 1940, and the accumulation of 4,000,000 yen in frozen funds. The association requests U.S. diplomatic representations to the Japanese government to secure the remaining import permits and protect American motion picture interests in future bilateral negotiations.

The association expresses gratitude for his initial mediation but protests that only $15,000 of the agreed $30,000 in film import permits have been granted despite full remittance of funds. Kaya's influence is solicited to expedite the remaining permits and preserve friendly relations between the Japanese government and the American motion picture industry.

It urges the Japanese authorities to release the remaining $12,500 in film import permits stipulated under the August 1938 agreement and highlights the disparity between Japanese restrictions on American films and the unrestricted entry of Japanese films into the United States. It also appeals for replacement permits for films rejected by censors and a more equitable allocation of quotas among member companies.
